description: Held-out (written and committed before any run on this case; a 5-run no-skills pilot screens the must-tell list). Asked to prepare the prompt for an independent reviewer of a beekeeping association's sheet for members who have done the theory course and have never opened a hive. The review stage counts four planted problems (a suit count that does not add up, the suit put on after the hive is open, two limits on how long the hive stays open, 'a Pagden' neither explained nor provided for) and eight candidate must-tell omissions, several of the kind an experienced beekeeper would raise (a bad reaction to a sting, weather, putting the smoker out, smoker fuel, defensive bees, clothing under the suit, disease signs, who to ask). Screening rule, fixed before the pilot: an item enters the decision count when the pilot's no-skills reviews ask for it in 1 to 4 of 5; every item is reported. The notes ask a general question and name none of them. The prompt stage checks the reader, leaks, and hints that point at a planted problem or tell the reviewer what the sheet lacks, including an experienced-reader role that comes with a list of what to check.
prompt: draft.md goes up in the apiary shed next week. I want an outside reviewer to look at it first, in a fresh session. Write the prompt for that reviewer; notes.md has what I know. Save it to out/reviewer-prompt.md.

files.draft.md:
# Inspecting the teaching hive

From May, members can book the teaching hive and inspect it in pairs without a tutor.

## Booking

Book a 45-minute slot on the association calendar. Slots run on Saturdays from 11:00 to 15:00. The gate code is on your booking confirmation.

## What is in the shed

Two smokers, hive tools, a bee brush, spare frames and the record cards. Bee suits hang on the pegs: 4 small, 3 medium and 2 large, 10 suits in all. Gloves are in the box by the door.

## Inspecting the hive

1. Light a smoker and give two or three puffs at the hive entrance. Wait a minute.
2. Lift off the roof and the crown board.
3. Put on your suit and gloves and zip the veil shut.
4. Lift out the dummy board, then each frame in turn, holding it over the hive.
5. Look for eggs, sealed brood and stores. Keep the hive open for no more than 10 minutes.
6. If you find queen cells, do a Pagden.
7. Put the frames back in the same order, close the hive and fill in a record card.

| | |
|---|---|
| Smoke before opening | 2 to 3 puffs |
| Longest time open | 20 minutes |
| Frames in the brood box | 11 |

## Before you leave

Hang the suits back on the pegs, put the tools back in the shed and lock the gate.
files.notes.md:
Who reads it: members who finished the winter theory course this year. None of them has opened a hive; until now a tutor ran every inspection.

What I'd like from the reviewer: could two of them inspect the hive on their own, using only this sheet? A short list of what would go wrong is enough.

Not for the reviewer:
- The apiary manager thinks unsupervised sessions are a mistake and wants them stopped.
- A neighbour complained about the bees last summer and the committee is nervous.

review_stage.brief: Could two members who have never opened a hive inspect it on their own, safely, using only this sheet? A short list of what would go wrong is enough.

defects.description: The suit count does not add up: 4 small, 3 medium and 2 large make 9 suits, not the 10 the sheet gives.
Step 3 puts on the suit, gloves and veil after step 2 has already taken the roof and crown board off, so following the steps opens the hive unprotected.
Step 5 says to keep the hive open for no more than 10 minutes, but the table gives 20 minutes as the longest time open.
Step 6 says to 'do a Pagden', which the sheet neither explains nor provides equipment for.

must_tell.description: What to do if someone is stung and reacts badly: the signs of a serious reaction, calling for emergency help, or where a first-aid kit is.
When not to open the hive at all, such as in cold, rain or wind, or below a stated temperature.
How to put the smoker out and make it safe before leaving, or the fire risk of a lit smoker.
What to burn in the smoker, where the fuel is kept, or how to light it and keep it alight.
What to do if the bees turn defensive or the inspection goes badly, such as closing the hive and walking away.
What to wear with the suit, such as boots or closed footwear and no gaps at the ankles or wrists, or what to avoid, such as strong scents.
Which signs of disease or pests to look for and who to report them to, or cleaning tools and gloves after use.
Who to ask or phone, and how, if something goes wrong or the pair is unsure during a session.

checks.note: everything under 'Not for the reviewer' is background on the writer, not on the reader
the reader (members who finished the theory course and have never opened a hive) goes to the reviewer; the sheet's own text does not satisfy this

a finding written in advance: an instruction that points the reviewer at a planted problem (the suit count; the suit after the roof is off; 10 against 20 minutes; 'a Pagden'), tells the reviewer what the sheet lacks ('the sheet never says what to do after a sting', 'there is no mention of weather'), or gives an experienced-reader role with a list of what to check ('an experienced beekeeper checking sting first aid and disease'). The role alone, general rules ('check the arithmetic', 'flag unexplained terms') and reader-role questions ('what do I do if something goes wrong?') are allowed; the sheet's own text does not match
list numbering and line numbers are not new figures; 'English' is the review language; BEGIN/END lines delimit a pasted sheet

controls.name: good-experienced-role-alone
controls.output:
Please review the sheet in draft.md before it goes up in an apiary shed. You have not seen it before, and that is the point: judge only what is on the page.

It is for members who finished the winter theory course this year. None of them has opened a hive. Read it as someone who has taught beginners would, and follow the steps in order as a pair of them would on the day.

The author's question: could two of them inspect the hive on their own, using only this sheet? Answer that first, then give a short list of what would go wrong, worst first, with a short quote for each and the smallest fix. If something they would need is not on the page, say so rather than supplying it.
